title: What a Burst Pipe Does to a House Over Days While Nobody Is Home | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: A day-by-day look at how a burst pipe spreads through an empty house, what to check first when you walk in, and what usually has to come out.
h1: What a Burst Pipe Does to a House Over Days When Nobody Is Home
breadcrumbLabel: Burst Pipe While Away From Home
intro: You opened the door expecting your house and got something else: standing water, a buckled floor, a smell that hits before you see anything. Nobody was here to catch it. Maybe it ran for two days, maybe for two weeks, and right now you are standing in the entry doing math you did not want to do. That is a lot to absorb in the first five minutes, and it is normal to just stand there for a while before you touch anything.

sections.heading: How the damage builds, hour by hour and then day by day
sections.body: A supply line under pressure does not trickle. A half-inch line can move several gallons a minute, continuously, until something shuts it off. In an occupied house, someone hears it. In an empty one, the water simply keeps going and the damage changes character as time passes. Understanding which stage you are in tells you a lot about what can be dried and what cannot.

cards.heading: Hours 1 to 6: spread and saturation
cards.body: Water finds the lowest path and travels along framing, under baseboards, and through the gaps around plumbing penetrations. Carpet pad acts like a sponge and wicks water horizontally well past the visible wet edge. Drywall pulls moisture upward from the floor several inches. At this stage almost everything is still salvageable if the water is clean.

cards.heading: Day 1 to Day 2: swelling and separation
cards.body: Particleboard and MDF (most cabinet boxes, vanity bases, and a lot of prefinished flooring cores) swell and lose structural integrity, and the swelling does not reverse when they dry. Laminate joints lift. Engineered wood cups. Baseboards pull away from walls. Wallpaper and paint start to release. Water that started clean has now picked up dirt, soap residue, and whatever was on the floor.

cards.heading: Day 2 to Day 4: mold and odor begin
cards.body: Mold generally needs moisture and organic material, and paper-faced drywall plus warm still air is close to ideal. In this window you start seeing growth on the back of baseboards, inside wall cavities, and on the underside of subfloor. The smell people describe as musty is the first sign, and it usually shows up before anything is visible.

cards.heading: Day 5 and beyond: structural and systems damage
cards.body: Sustained saturation delaminates subfloor plywood and can loosen fasteners in framing. Water in a ceiling cavity puts real weight overhead. Insulation compresses and stops working. Electrical boxes, outlets, and any HVAC ducting the water reached become questions for a professional rather than judgment calls you should make yourself.

sections.heading: What to do in the first hour after you find it
sections.body:
None of this has to happen perfectly. Do what you can and leave the rest.

Shut the water off at the main. In most Phoenix-area homes the main shutoff is on the exterior wall near the front hose bib, in a box near the street, or in the garage. If you find the specific broken line, its local stop valve works too.

Do not walk into standing water if it is anywhere near outlets, a panel, or appliances. If you can safely reach the breaker box while standing on a dry surface, kill power to the affected areas. If you cannot, leave it and stay out.

Take photos and video before you move anything. Wide shots of each room, then close shots of the failure point, wet flooring, and any damaged contents. This is the record your insurance adjuster will work from, and it is much easier to get now than to reconstruct later.

Call your insurance carrier and open a claim. Ask specifically whether the policy covers sudden discharge and what documentation they want. Then stop. You do not have to start tearing anything out today.

sections.heading: How the drying and repair work actually goes
sections.body: There are two distinct phases, and people often think they are one. Mitigation is stopping the damage and drying the structure. Reconstruction is putting the house back. The first happens fast, the second takes longer and is a different kind of work. Mitigation means extracting standing water, removing materials that cannot be dried (usually carpet pad, saturated drywall in a controlled cut, wet insulation, swollen cabinet bases), and then setting air movers and dehumidifiers to pull moisture out of framing and subfloor. Moisture meters and readings taken over several days are what determine when it is actually dry, not how it looks or feels. Wall cavities are frequently dried with drilled ports or a small controlled removal so air can reach behind the surface. Reconstruction is drywall, texture, paint, trim, flooring, and cabinetry. On a long-running leak it can also mean subfloor replacement or framing repair. Matching existing finishes matters here, and it is worth asking how a contractor handles transitions where new flooring meets old. If you want to see how each side of this works, there is more detail on water damage restoration and on reconstruction and rebuild.

sections.heading: Keeping it from happening the next time you leave
sections.body:
This is worth reading once things settle, not today.

Shut the main off before any trip longer than a weekend. It costs nothing and it ends this entire category of problem. If you have an irrigation system or an ice maker you want running, isolate those separately.

Replace braided supply lines on toilets, sinks, and washing machines on a schedule rather than waiting for failure. The rubber inside them degrades even when the braid looks fine. Water heaters, especially past the ten-year mark, are a common source of the kind of slow flood that goes unnoticed.

In Arizona, summer heat matters more than freezing. Attic-run PEX and CPVC, and hose bibs left pressurized in direct sun, take real thermal stress. Check attic lines and the water heater pan for staining once a year.

A leak sensor under each sink and behind the washer, plus an automatic shutoff valve on the main, is the closest thing to a real answer for a house that sits empty. They are widely available and not expensive relative to what one incident costs.

faqs.q: How long can water sit before mold becomes a problem?
faqs.a: General industry guidance puts the start of mold growth on wet organic materials in roughly the first two to three days under normal indoor temperatures. Arizona homes are often warm inside even when nobody is there, which does not slow it down. If the leak ran longer than that, assume the wall cavities and subfloor need to be opened and checked rather than just dried from the surface.

faqs.q: The floor looks dry now. Is it actually fine?
faqs.a: Often not. Surfaces dry first while the framing, subfloor, and the inside of wall cavities hold moisture for much longer. That trapped moisture is what causes odor and growth weeks later. The only reliable way to know is moisture readings taken in the material itself, and those should be repeated over several days rather than taken once.

faqs.q: Should I start pulling out wet carpet and drywall myself?
faqs.a: You can, but photograph everything first and check with your adjuster, because removing material before it is documented can complicate a claim. Also be careful about what you cut into: water that has been sitting for days may be contaminated, and there may be wiring in the walls you cannot see. Extraction and controlled demolition are usually faster and cleaner with the right equipment.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover a burst pipe in an empty house?
faqs.a: Policies commonly cover sudden and accidental water discharge, but some have exclusions or conditions related to vacancy, unoccupied periods, or failure to maintain heat or shut off water. Read your policy language and ask your carrier directly about the specific circumstances. Your documentation of when you left and when you returned can matter.
